utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please take a chair. Any preliminary matters that you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You mean, you do not want me to introduce ourselves any more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good afternoon, to you. Appearances the Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm with David Cunningham, Aleksandar Vujic, and Cynthia Dresden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you and good afternoon to you too. Okay. The documentation, we have most of it here. The problem, almost had altercations with the Registrar today because of the limited space we have in this courtroom to be able to have all the documents of this case. But anyway, should we require more than we have, then we will see how to go about it. Preliminaries. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm confused and I must say distressed regarding this particular witness that is coming here today, and we need to go into private session, I suppose, to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session to discuss it. To discuss what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman, very shortly we will be starting with the testimony of BT94, who is being recalled by the Trial Chamber, still a Prosecution witness. Reason why we have decided to recall him is that going through his testimony and also his diary, we did come to the conclusion that there were several matters that we preferred to have clarified, and also several other questions that we would like to put arising out of his testimony and combined with his diary. The result of this, we came to this conclusion rather after we sat together and we discussed. We then elaborated, each Judge separately first, a list of questions that we wanted to put to this witness. These have been collated in one set. I will be conducting the examination in the first place. As we go along, since this is a combined effort, as we go along and while he is answering, say, the first question, it may well be that Judge Janu or Judge Taya may have additional questions. So we will continue like this. In other words, I'll start, but there may be additional questions arising out of the questions or of the answer which may be forthcoming from myself and the other two Judges, all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then at the end, as we agreed on the sitting of the 28th of January, you will both have opportunities to put questions to the witness on matters arising out of the questions and answers -- questions that were put and his answers to us. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first may I say, Your Honours may have noticed Ms. Sutherland's hurried arrival in this courtroom, but just for the purposes of the record she's here. Secondly, in what order, Your Honour? Will it be cross-examination, as it were, or examination by Mr. Ackerman and then re-examination by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not that important for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would have thought that it makes -- I would suggest it makes more sense. Because if he remains our witness, then Mr. Ackerman has the right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think the way I see it, the logical way of seeing it, is that once we have finished with our questions and answers, I think I would give the witness back to you, and then Mr. Ackerman can cross-examine arising out of our questions - it's not exactly a cross-examination, but arising out of your questions. Yes, that could be referred to as cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was saying it was the other way around. But you ask the questions first, then Mr. Ackerman, and then I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. re-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I was thinking of we go first, obviously, and then you go immediately afterwards, and then Mr. Ackerman have re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I mean. He's not actually Mr. Ackerman's witness. He's actually a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly so you go first after us. And then he goes last.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I get two bites at the cherry, then, if I re-examine. That's what I mean. This is the slight complication. Your Honours are asking the questions and have called him back. Arising out of that, the normal thing would be, when Your Honours ask questions, you ask either party whether they have any questions arising out of that. Normally then the Defence would go first and the Prosecution go second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he is a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. So I go last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I would do it the opposite way. But anyway, if this is how you prefer it, this is how --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, he's a Prosecution witness, she has to go first. That's just the way it is. You're absolutely right, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is exactly what -- this is how I see it. I think you go first immediately after us, and then he goes last.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the whole point, Your Honour, then I get two chances, because I get a chance to re-examine after -- do you see what I mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, yes. Okay, all right. But I think that's of minor importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have no particular objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's of minor importance. But I think we were talking at cross-purposes. So I think we need to go into private session while he walks in, no? Or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, that doesn't help because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because of the facial distortion and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hope they have worked on it. Your Honour, if it's in private session, then if there was somebody in the public gallery, they could see him come in. So We would have to go into closed and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Honestly, I can't see behind the glass, tainted glass. But I don't think there is anyone there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in that case, Your Honour he can come in and then the facial distortion...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Security has been informed before the hearing start that we're going into this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. So let's bring the witness in, please. And whoever is responsible for --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can we just pause for one minute so they can fix the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we remain in open session while he walks in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am pretty sure you were not expecting to see us again. But welcome back to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know the procedure. You're going to be handed the text of a solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that's your undertaking with us that you will be telling the truth in the course of your testimony. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a chair. And let's start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me explain to you first and foremost why you are here once more. You testified last year in May and June -- in June, I think. May and June. And recently we were through your testimony, and also examining the details of your diary. And since then, of course, we have also heard several other witnesses, and therefore we have had the benefit of evidence on several matters that you touched upon in your testimony which are recorded in your diary, or events which you did not touch upon in your testimony, and we decided that it's the case of asking you to come back here so that you can help us clear up our minds on several issues. I don't want to alarm you unduly. You will not be here for days at length. I think your testimony will last maybe a day or two, after which you will be able to go home. But before we start with the testimony, I want to make sure of a couple of things. When did you arrive here in The Hague? When did you get here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On Monday. Before you came here, were you approached by anyone with regard to the subject matter of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Since you became aware that you were going to be recalled to give testimony, did anyone speak to you while you -- before you had arrived here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was only told that I had to come here, Your Honour. But no one explained why. No one gave any explanations to that effect, and I arrived here on Monday at about 11.30, here in The Hague. And I was only given my diary to look at it. And yesterday and today, I had a chance at looking at some tapes. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who spoke to you since your arrival here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only Maria Kavall, and Kellie for maybe some 15 minutes. I spoke for some five minutes with my dear Prosecutor, Joanna, but she never seems to have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why is she your dear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand, I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why is she your dear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. She is a good person. She is nice, and she always understood me. She understood how much effort I invested into the things that I did. And it was only in this sense that I meant this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when did you meet Ms. Korner since your arrival here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was yesterday, and only for some five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And apart from Ms. Korner, did you meet anyone else from the Prosecution team?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He just told you, Your Honour. He met an investigator, and the interpreter who he called Maria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maria is an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: She is an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the investigator is?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Kellie Ward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you ask you what you discussed with Kellie Ward, with the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, we mostly talked about my testimony. I was watching the tapes of my previous testimony, and that's what we mostly talked about. We also touched upon some of the details relating to the copy of my diary that had been sent to me. And that's about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was the subject matter of the discussion? You were reviewing your testimony on video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And was he present all the time while you were reviewing this testimony? Sorry, she. Was she present all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was with Maria. She was in charge of it, this interpreter, whereas Kellie would only show up for a minute or two, ask me if I needed a coffee or if I wanted to go and have a smoke, because I'm a passionate smoker, and that's why she would come. And I had this feeling that she was controlling whether we were really reviewing the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But did you discuss the contents of your testimony with Ms. Kellie Ward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, no. I was under the impression that Kellie was pretty satisfied with my testimony. We did not discuss it. She only wanted to make sure that I took a good look at it to remind myself, to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who gave you -- did you bring again a copy of your diary with you, or were you given a copy of it here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a copy of the diary back home, and that is the copy that they had sent to me, and that's what we discussed, as I've already said. I did not have, however, a copy of the video containing my testimony. I was only given it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ask Ms. Ward or anyone else for that matter to be handed any other documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I know that, in principle, I am not entitled to this, and whatever she is aware that can be given to me, she would give it to me. So I did not receive any of the documents, but I was shown -- I was shown, I think, two or three videotapes containing some material, news reports and so on, produced by the Banja Luka TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Had you seen these video reports before in your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, in Banja Luka, while I was still there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But were you shown anything or any kind of evidence that you were not aware of before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to tell you frankly, I had seen all these reports previously, and I was surprised to see how few materials there were. I was surprised. They did, however, tell me that there were other tapes, but that there wasn't enough time for them to show them to me. So I watched two tapes, in addition to my testimony, which had nothing to do with the goings-on in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who suggested that you see -- watch these two videos, these tapes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought I had made that clear. That was my instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him... Was it you or Ms. Kellie --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't personally show them. But I mean, you know, the witness may have been shown by Ms. Ward, but I want to make absolutely clear that it was my instruction he be shown these videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What were you told when you were asked to -- or when you were invited to watch these videos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They asked me whether I had seen these footages before. I said yes. And then they asked me who the journalist was, and I told them. I told them the journalists' names before they would appear on the screen, and that was all. And it was only with Maria that I was watching these videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you at any time discuss with any of the member of the team for the Prosecution your testimony of today and of tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not. I even expected to meet Ms. Joanna today, but she told me that she was unable to meet with me before the end of my testimony. (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's suspend the sitting for three minutes, four minutes. We go outside and we come back. The witness can leave the courtroom, and we'll get him back when we tell you. --- Break taken at 2.59 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to make an application. I understand it's objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What application?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That part of the last answer given by the witness relating to -- can we go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: After two years, I still have the template with the name of Judge Hunt. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you just asked me if I had anything to say about the questions he was asked and answers that he gave. I think you asked him very clearly about any conversations that he had with representatives of the Prosecutor's Office. He obviously was not truthful to you, if Joanna Korner's emails to us are truthful, they talk about things that he -- conversations that he had with the Prosecutor and things that he told the Prosecutor that he didn't tell you when you asked him that open-ended question, so I think already he started out being untruthful. And my submission is that's the way he has been since the day he came here, first day. But that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I suppose you have nothing else to add, Ms. Korner. Our decision is as follows: We refer you in the first place to the debate we had here on the -- in the sitting of the 28th of January. And what happened on that day was that Ms. Korner rose and said: "The only question is this. Your Honours dismissed him, is he allowed to review the evidence he gave before Your Honours, however many months ago it was before he comes back. I think it would probably be better if he did because that -- then he would have some idea. But as I'm not entirely sure the status, Your Honour, he remains our witness, of course, and we are bringing him back at Your Honours' request for further questions. He was given an opportunity to review his original statement before he testified the first time, plus obviously the documents. Is he permitted to review his testimony then?" There was some exchange of discussion. And I'm reported as saying: "But I see no problem in that. Do you see any problems, Judge Taya, Judge Janu?" This doesn't show in the record, but there was no problem on the part of my two colleagues. Then I said: "Yes, it's even better because basically we will be asking him some questions, and the reason why we want to ask him questions is having gone through his evidence here, there are some points that we need clarification upon." And then Ms. Korner said: "Your Honour, having asked the questions, then effectively allow Mr. Ackerman if anything arises to re-cross-examine and myself to re-examine." And I said: "Yes, it's normal practice. If there's anything arising from the questions we put and what his answers are, if there is anything that is new, fresh or requires some kind of intervention from Mr. Ackerman or from yourself Ms. Korner, we will allow for that. Yes, so that's the position. Is there anything else?" And that was almost the end of the discussion, except that there is another excerpt in which Ms. Korner says: "BT94 will be here, arriving on Monday, so allowing him Tuesday to refresh his memory for his testimony, he will be available for Your Honours Wednesday morning and whenever we are sitting." What happened afterwards may not have been exactly as we had intended it to be when we communicated to the Prosecution and to Defence, that it was our wish that he be advised of the subject matter or more or less the main topic that he would be asked upon. But we have heard the witness here answer the questions that we put to him, and we are satisfied that there is no contamination and no irregularity of substance that could convince us to accede to your request that you put earlier, Mr. Ackerman. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to thank you very much for bringing that exchange from the record to our attention and making it part of the record of this particular hearing. And I will just say that it's very clear that from that hearing, the Prosecution was given permission to let him look at his prior testimony, not given permission to start showing him new material, which is exactly what they did, never done with permission of this Chamber. That's the part I'm objecting to. I don't care if he reads his prior testimony, and I don't care if he reads his diary, but for the Prosecution to start showing him new material without any permission from the Court, without any response from me, I think is improper. If the Prosecution had said at that time that, "We would like to additionally show him some new material, Your Honours," then I probably would have objected to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow this to go on the record like this. Your Honours know, and Mr. Ackerman knows, and he's deliberately ignoring it. That had that been -- had there been no further communication, that is the way it would have been. He would have reviewed his testimony in his diary. Mr. Ackerman knows that Your Honours sent both of us an email, or via your legal officer an email saying it should be communicated to him. And I have explained exactly what was done as a result. And as I say, for the third time, I could have sat on this information, and I find it infamous that the accusations are now being levelled, again, that I am deliberately interfering with testimony given by witnesses when in fact I informed, as is my want throughout this whole case, the Chamber and Mr. Ackerman of exactly what had passed. And I think the time has come to stop this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Ms. Korner. May I also make it public that we three are also convinced that there absolutely no ulterior motives on your part beyond what we had indicated we needed to. The way we understand it is the following: That the moment we sent out the message to you loud and clear, both of you, that the majority of the questions will be directed on propaganda, it was only natural and logical to assume that the questions that we would be asking the witness on propaganda would also be based on information that -- on evidence that has been tendered and received by this Tribunal since his testimony here. And the thing is that we do not see any contamination here or any irregularity of substance that should stop us from proceeding with the questioning of this witness. So let's proceed. BT94, please. Again, we remain in open session even while he walks in. Yeah, yeah, but it changes from courtroom to courtroom. So in Courtroom III or Courtroom I, we would do it differently. So let's continue. It's important that he has available before him -- in front, on his desk, the copy of his diary, Madam Chuqing. Is it already available? And there's a transcript of his testimony. That would be extremely helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He can't read it. It's in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have it in B/C/S, he won't be able to read. It's in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He doesn't understand English at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. That's why we had him watching the videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will be referring to lines specific to you, and so both Mr. Ackerman and yourself, Ms. Korner, should be able to follow me. But that escaped me. I do not have the corresponding reference in -- you do have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's try it. If it doesn't work, we will have to find a solution. I was acting under the presumption that the witness knew some English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can hear Madam Registrar saying that if it goes onto the ELMO, the specific page that Your Honours are referring to, so the translators can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start with the first question. I'm going to refer you to your testimony of the 23rd of June of last year. And at page 17.997, 17.997 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the interpreters have not been provided with the documents, and we are unable to give you the exact quotes. We can only interpret what we hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely how it's going to be. So we can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can put it up through Sanction on to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's even better. That's even better. And at line 17.997, you are reported to have testified as follows: "Well, a bad influence, not just on the citizens, on the urban part, but particularly on the rural part. It had a catastrophic influence. They were convinced they were under threat, and every word that was uttered through the media represented a law to them."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, in addition to that, at page 18.160 of the transcript, with particular reference, and perhaps you can check this to your entry in your diary referring to the 10th of June of 1992, you also said -- you also said: "Not a single positive word about Muslims can be read or heard in the local media. When they are all Islamic fundamentalists, extremists, or fanatics."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We came to the conclusion reading this that they were sweeping statements of a generic nature. Can you be more specific? Let's take them one by one. On what basis do you tell us or do you believe that this propaganda was deleterious had a really bad influence, not just on citizens on the urban part but particularly in the rural part, it had a catastrophic influence. On what authority do you state this, do you make this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: You see, Your Honour, in the former Yugoslavia, we all lived following the principle of brotherhood and unity, and we truly believed that we were all brothers. And I still maintain that we are. We all belong to the same people, except that one part of that population was -- became orthodox, and the other Catholic. It was not an empty space. We all belonged to the same people, but we belonged to three different religions. Now, when someone tells me I'm from Bosnia, I'm from Bosnia the same way as the Pope is. I am a Catholic, but I'm also a Bosnian. Now, why is it that I made that conclusion? You see, after the life that we had enjoyed for years, it was necessary to use what was missed by the communists. We had to solve the burdens of the past. We still lived with those burdens. We didn't know anything at that time. And the new Messiahs, whom we had unfortunately elected without having properly analysed them beforehand, we were not aware of who they really were, all of a sudden started to talk to us about being in danger, being in jeopardy. And it was necessary to demonise the opposite side for -- in order to convince me that my neighbours with whom I had lived for years are now my enemies. So this is -- this is my opinion. And there are countless examples for that. What you mentioned, the 10th of June, I read in the papers -- with your permission, I should like to read to you just one thing which is very difficult to understand. I mean, for the people who come from normal countries, such as you. But please, try to understand this. "A prayer to Thoreau".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slowly, because I think the interpreters have having difficulties to catch up with you. So you can start this again, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I'm not receiving interpretation. I didn't receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was trying for explain to you that the interpreters are finding it difficult to catch up with you. And if you could kindly start all over again with this "prayer to."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: "While I'm still of sound mind, I pray to you, St. Vitus. St. Vitus, who can see from the heavens everything that people on the earth are not aware of, I pray to you to save my brethren whose pain can be seen in their -- at their homes."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I just --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: "I am hurting all over because of the pain that was caused to us by the enemy."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If the witness pauses, he's actually reading, Your Honour, it may help the interpreters and Your Honours, he's reading from the end of the entry which is for the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is something that's recorded in his diary. If the interpreters have the diary, it's the very last part of the entry for the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Here, we're talking about martyrs that have been slaughtered, and it's very painful for me to read this. And when the population generally speaking is faced with such texts on a daily basis, then obviously they will feel in danger. I'm not exaggerating anything. There was constant talk about people slaughtered, killed, murdered. It's -- once again, it's very painful and sickening for me to go on. And maybe on the very next day, here in the next entry, you have the following: "The Serb TV and the Radio Banja Luka have to be much stronger in the propaganda. The radio must repeatedly broadcast the news from the borders of Yugoslavia so that all listeners could hear them, despite frequent power shortages." So you have this constant repetition, and you know, Your Honours, that once a lie is broadcasted and once these broadcasts become frequent, then it's very difficult to see the truth for those who are exposed to such broadcasts. And this is why I stated that the media had killed, symbolically speaking, a number of people before so many people were actually killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you still haven't explained to us why you draw the distinction between, say, citizens living in the urban sections of the country and those living --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- in the rural part. Why do you make such distinction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: The difference is a drastic one. I don't think that such huge differences can be found anywhere else. It is mostly mixed population that lives in towns. It is perfectly normal for me to come across a Muslim friend or a Serb friend out in the street. There were many mixed marriages. There are still many children from mixed marriages. The population was completely mixed in urban areas. Needless to say, the level of education was much higher in towns than in villages where most of the population worked on the land. There was another characteristic of Bosnia which was quite important, especially in cases of villages where only one nationality lived. It was very difficult to delude the people. This was often done by local priests who frequently played rather dishonourable roles in our society, which was not the case in cities and in towns. In villages, the local population regularly attended church services. The churches were always packed, whereas in towns the churches were places where you could go in on a hot day and rest in the shade. So once again, the urban population was always better educated than the rural one. And that is the reason why it was so easy to delude the rural population with the stories of martyrs and saviors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But arising out of this, how easy was it for the people living in rural parts to have access to the media? Because we have had witnesses here telling us how difficult it was, either because of electricity or because of money, that...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: You see, the press, generally speaking, the print media, people no longer regularly bought newspapers because they were very poor. As for the electronic media, of course, we had television and we had radio as well. And there were constant broadcasts over the radio and the TV of that nature. And it was easy to overcome the problem of power shortages as well because there were generators. We constantly used generators to listen to the radio or to watch TV. And both radio and TV constantly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. repeated one and the same story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One final question on this area: How frequent, according to your -- according to you, were these statements in the local media labelling Muslims as Islamic fundamentalists, extremists, or fanatics, and can you recall specific instances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can, Your Honour. This was a common occurrence, an everyday phenomena. Of course, one would from time to time be surprised at reading something normal. There were also, so to speak, good Muslims and good Croats. However, in most of the cases, such as here, for instance, and I'm looking at a declaration which says: "Serbs and all honourable Krajina people, let us stand up and defend our freedom, our religion, and our homes. We are fighting against Ustasha and Islamic fascists. We are fighting lies and international conspiracy. We're fighting for the truth, and we cannot lose." This is what you were able to hear after every news broadcast. And then again, the following: "Let us understand, we are not under the blockade by the 6th American Fleet, but by Zulja and Mulja from Gracac town, and from Urja and Bjura [phoen] from Placa. May they all die or get killed by a bullet. That is the kind of justice that they deserve." Now, this is the kind of speech that you could hear in the media. This is the level and the type of news that you could hear in the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you could just ask him to identify the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, I was going to ask him precisely that. Where are you reading from? Where can we find this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: This is the entry of the 20th of June 1992. Page number 021058. And if this is what was in place in 1992, then you can just imagine how things were in 1993. The international conspiracy was entered in under the date of 18th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the second question. And this should be a very simple, straightforward one. Please, Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman, refer to page 17.998 of the transcript. And that's relative to the testimony of the witness tendered on the 23rd of June of 2003. Sir, while you were testifying on the 23rd of June 2003, you gave as an example a live, phone-in radio programme dealing with NATO air strikes, air strike threats, where the programme's host, a certain Milenko Stojicic --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- did absolutely nothing, did not lift a finger to placate a listener who had phoned in threatening the Muslims from Sanski Most. And you added during your testimony that this programme and this intervention by this listener and nonintervention by Milenko Stojicic was followed by a an attack on a mosque in Potok and a stabbing in Rudarska Street of a man --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, the mosque in Potocka. The Potocka Dzamija, that's what it's called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the stabbing in Rudarska Street of a man over whose corpse a Koran was placed. Now, what I need you to clear for us, to clarify for us is the following: We need to place this within a time frame. Do you know when this happened? I'm telling you, sir, why, because we are only concerned with events that took place within a certain time frame. So I want to make sure whether this falls within that time frame, or whether it's an event which took place afterwards or before. If I can be of any help, because this is what prompted us to have this question put to you, in one of the statements that you made, that you gave to the Prosecution, and I'm referring to Exhibit Number P2342.2 -- sorry, P2324.2 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure what you're referring to. Was his witness statement made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it was made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know but it was made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. That was the time Your Honour was giving me an hour and a half to -- that's why. I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. If you give me the statement, I will read out from here to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If it's tendered under seal, we have to go into closed session -- we still have to go into closed session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, the only reason it's tendered under seal, it's not for the contents, so long as it doesn't identify him, his name, there's no reason why it shouldn't be read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can show it to him and then he can explain to us or confirm whether this is the same incident or is it a different one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, it reads here: Wednesday, 1st of September 1993. That's when the programme was broadcast. And I was talking about it on Thursday, 2nd of September 1993 when we were all aware of the consequences. The mosque was shot at. Nermin Djumisic was killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you. I just wanted to confirm. Mr. Ackerman, do you want to see this statement? Mr. Ackerman? Do you want to see this statement? I just wanted to confirm actually the impression we had that this was an incident that occurred in 1993 and not in 1992. All right. And incidentally, just for the record, it transpires that the translation into English of his statement, Ms. Korner, 1st September, 1993, was erroneously indicated as 1st September 1998, but we are satisfied that it is 1993 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this the only instance that you recall of an event like this happening --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: No, no, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- happening -- let me finish, please. Happening after a TV or radio programme, or are you aware of other incidents that took place which you attribute as a direct result of the transmission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: In my humble opinion, everything that happened was a result of TV or radio programmes. At this very moment, I cannot recall any such event, but there were many such events. Initially, we had the normal TV programmes, but then the Serb rebels captured the relay in Kozara to ostensibly give us the true information as opposed to Sarajevo where lies came from. And it was then that their truth started coming out, which was to have its climax in the TV Banja Luka programme which, prior to every news -- Krajina news programme, would broadcast the "moments of truth," as they called them. There, you were able to see repeatedly slaughtered corpses, dead bodies. The commentary was that Serbs were biologically endangered. What does it mean? They never said who they were endangered by but they always pointed to those on the other side being Ustashas and Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stick to the question and not deviate from it. We are agreed that you are referring here to an incident or a sequence of incidents that took place in September 1993. We are not actually interested as such in the event except insofar as you hint in your testimony a link between what was threatened during the programme by this listener and what happened subsequently. Do you believe in this link, to start with? Are you so sure in your mind that the stabbing of this gentleman in Rudarska Street and the attack on the mosque in Potok occurred because someone had threatened the people of the -- the non-Serbs of Sanski Most? Or could they have happened independently of that threat? What's your position on that? Let's start from here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I'm certain that there is a direct link between the two, and there is no doubt about it. Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop there as far as regards this incident. Prior to September 1993, and relatively to the period April 1992 to December 1992, are you aware of any incidents occurring as, in your mind, a direct link or a direct result of what was stated in the media? Please be specific. I don't want you to be generic, because being generic doesn't help us in the least.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Well, this is quite difficult for me because whatever has been written down here, many of these things it's very difficult to remember; I forget them. What I know is that we lived a normal life, and as soon as these stories came out, people started losing their lives. Now, as for specific examples, I am really unable at this stage to recall any. Had I known that this would be asked of me, I would have taken some time in the hotel yesterday evening to take a look at the entries and maybe refresh my memory, but I couldn't know what you were going to ask me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously. I mean, we couldn't tell you the questions. But perhaps you will have time later on today, this evening, and tomorrow morning to try and refresh your memory. If you can recall any of such instances, please do come back to us tomorrow. If you don't, also come back to us tomorrow and tell us that you don't recall any specific incidents like this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please refer to transcript page number T18.166. Now, I'm going to read out to you part of your testimony here given on the 24th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: We don't have it on the screen, the number. No, it is okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is okay. And then I'm going to ask you a series of questions because this short paragraph of about five lines contains several statements. You state as follows. You were describing the role of the media at that time which is relevant for our case in Banja Luka and in Bosnia-Herzegovina as follows. You said: "The media were not calling for genocide, but were creating an atmosphere which led to the misfortune that occurred. It's the media's fault most of all."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Who would have heard Mr. Brdjanin speak had it not been for Radio Banja Luka, TV Banja Luka, TV Pale if the local newspapers hadn't been there? It was the media that paved the way. They paved the way for what eventually happened to our deepest regret." Now, I realise that you have touched on some of these aspects when answering the previous questions that I put to you, but I would like you to be more specific. Let's start with the first part of your statement. "The media were not calling for genocide, but were creating an atmosphere which led to the misfortune that occurred." What is the difference? Or what would be the difference in your mind when you say that there was no specific calling for genocide, but there was this creation of an atmosphere which led to the misfortune that occurred? What do you mean by that? We know more or less the misfortune that occurred. I mean, this is a matter that everyone knows, the sad events that took place throughout the whole decade, throughout the whole war. But what do you want to tell us here? Do you want to tell us that -- let's say what you want to tell us, and then I -- if necessary, I will put another question to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: When I said that they did not directly call for it, well, you could not hear anyone say, "Let's go and kill everyone in the village. Let's raze Srebrenica to the ground. Let's destroy them." Well, there was no such thing. Similarly, in this earlier example related to the unfortunate Sanski Most, it wasn't the presenter who would call upon the people to do what eventually happened, but by addressing the people in a savage way, addressing their lower savage senses, instincts, this created a psychosis, a climate that favoured the atrocious events that happened. They did not try to ease the tensions, to calm things down, to tell people to stop for a second and think about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a case here where the accused is being charged with genocide. You're telling us that the media were not calling for genocide but were creating an atmosphere which led to the misfortune that occurred. What misfortune are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I was referring to the whole of my Bosnia. The whole of Bosnia was a misfortune. That is how I look at it. I repeat: You wouldn't hear anyone on the radio calling upon people to go and commit crimes but they allowed people who did call for violence to speak up at the radio or TV, if I've put myself clearly. So the media have enabled these hawks to promote themselves, to take -- to take centre stage, and that's what was so catastrophic about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you mean to tell us, because this needs to be clear, that in your mind the media were not calling for genocide but were creating an atmosphere which led to genocide?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but Your Honour, I'm concerned that there may be a muddling of concepts. One is the legal concept of genocide, which may not be the concept of genocide that he's talking about, so in order to clarify, if I may suggest, to ask him what he means by genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I want to know from the witness is precisely whether he's telling us -- the media never said, "Let's kill them all," but created an atmosphere which practically meant, so was sending a message, "Let's kill them all." Not as loud and clear as it would have been had it been loud and clear, and this is what I want to hear from you, whether you equivolate the misfortune that occurred, whether you equivolate -- we need to know this, whether you were equivolating what you mention as the misfortune that occurred with what in your mind amounts to genocide? Are you telling us the media never said, "We are calling for genocide," but equally created an atmosphere which couldn't but lead to genocide? Is this what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely. That is precisely what I wanted to say. Under the guise of neutrality, they would give a chance to people to speak up for whom they knew what they would say, that they would appeal to the basic -- to the base instincts of the multitude of people. So they would pave the way, and if you could say this was done in gloves, so to speak, in an indirect way for the people to commit genocide. And these are the people that I hold responsible. I think that they are directly responsible for what happened. But this is the distinction that I make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You continue by saying that practically nothing of the sort would have happened had it not been for the media. Is this what you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Janu would like put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Witness, following the media day after day, could you spot that there was a plan or there was a management after all this propaganda?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: This could easily be seen far before the outbreak of the conflict. One could follow the developments and the direction where they were headed. Even before anyone was aware of the magnitude of the catastrophe that would ensue, you could see that the press changed its tone. They talked about Serbs being endangered, how all the other peoples were to blame for the fact that the Serbs were left behind, they were the ones who had fewer votes in the assembly, and that is how they started creating the atmosphere of them being endangered by others. And this atmosphere spread from Croatia to Bosnia. And Croats from -- Croats in Bosnia failed to realise that they were basically misused by the leaders. And that was also true for the Serbs, because they were placing all their hopes in Belgrade. Everyone was involved in this game, and then suddenly the leaders emerged in the foreground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So do I understand you well that it was coming from one centre and spreading through the country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, it started from Belgrade. I think this is a fact of common knowledge. It started out in Belgrade and spread from there further. The Serbian Academy of Arts, the SANU, they planted the story about the Serbs being endangered for the sake of the world, and that is something that the common people did not understand. They needed pawns, and they allowed these pawns to be raised to high-level positions to implement this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stop here for the time being. My apologies to everybody, I was under the impression that we would have the break at quarter past 4.00, I didn't realise it should have been at quarter to 4.00. So my apologies, we will have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just inquire, and it's partly for the purpose of the witness, because I'm afraid that we were all under a complete misunderstanding, which is that he would be here for about an hour today. Your Honours will be going into tomorrow on questions with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, it's all right, Your Honour. We have to obviously -- arrangements have to be made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Initially I had thought we would finish today. But probably we will need a small part of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's fine. It's just that I know that -- I think arrangements were made on a misunderstanding that he was going back tomorrow and that he wouldn't be required again. So I hope that the investigators are watching.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just ask, I'm sorry, again, it's my fault, I was under a completely false impression. Would Your Honours say, then, that you won't be sitting beyond 6.30 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I never said that, but if you want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking if Your Honours would do that. It simply never occurred to me, and I made arrangements which I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem, Ms. Korner. It's okay. We will sit up to 6.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay with you, Mr. Ackerman? Okay. Let me take you back again to the topic that we were -- you're not finished. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Yes, Judge Janu has some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Sir, you were telling us about the involvement of academics from the academy of science in this propaganda business. Do you remember some names? Some leading personalities who were engaged in this process?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Of course I do. The entire Academy of Arts and Sciences, the Belgrade-based Academy of Arts and Sciences, first they publicised the memorandum, the infamous memorandum, and then a number of their members, Cosic, Betkovic, and others, they were all working on the same agenda. They wanted to appeal to the people living in Bosnia to convince them of the fact that Serbia was in danger, that everyone was against Serbia, and so on and so forth. The writers' club located at Francuska Street number 7 were all working towards the same goal. All of a sudden, a number of books were published that were speaking to the same idea. And the people followed like blind. They turned their back to their neighbours because they believed those intellectuals. And this is how it all started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So those people, those intellectuals, had quite a big space in the media to present their views and opinions? Are you telling us this? And, sir, I believe that as in any nation, there were Serbian intellectuals who had quite opposite view. Did you, following the media, did you witness that those people for balancing the opinion had the space in the media to express what they thought about the problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I followed the media. However, those honourable people, such the former mayor of Belgrade, Mr. Bogdan Bogdanovic, they did not have any space in the media. They were all rejected. They were no longer there. They were absent. All of a sudden, they disappeared. And you had a new range of smart people, so to speak, who were ostensibly telling the truth. They were given the space in the media. They were on TV, and the population, generally speaking, looked up to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Did you come across the name Vladimir Srebrov, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Of course I did. According to my knowledge, he was the founder of the Serbian Democratic Party. And later, when he realised what it had turned into, he abandoned the party. And at one point, he was even arrested by the Serbs. He suffered a lot. I'm aware of that. He went through a terrible ordeal, and in the end he turned out to be quite an honourable man, despite the fact that he was the founder of the Serbian Democratic Party, Vladimir Srebrov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While we are -- rather, I'm taking you back to the media. You said it was the media's fault most of all. During the period in question, 1992, in particular, April to December, in particular, which newspapers are you aware of that existed, that were published?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I believe I was aware of all of them, except that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we have a list of them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: For instance, in Banja Luka, if you're referring to Banja Luka specifically, you were able to buy Glas, Srpski, the paper called Javnost, published by the SDS. You were also able to buy all Belgrade-based papers. However, nothing from Zagreb or Sarajevo. And this is how the truth was presented. We had no alternatives. We did not have other papers to compare and to be able to draw our own conclusions. We had access to Belgrade-based papers, plus the Glas from Banja Luka, which was later called Glas Srpski, and some others. Those were the print media that we had access to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why was that so? Was it because there were no papers from Sarajevo and from Zagreb, or for some other reasons that they were not available?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: If anyone caught you reading the Oslobodjenje from Sarajevo, you would be beaten up. Those were simply prohibited papers. It was not possible to read those papers during that period of time. To read papers coming from some other part of the country, the opinion -- the public opinion generally speaking was uniform. There was only one truth, which was presented to us in this manner. We now know to what extent this was actually true, the information that they were presenting. But in those days, those were the papers that were reaching Banja Luka. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were there any clandestine publications that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: You mean if anything was printed illegally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by the Muslims or by the Croats, or by the non-Serbs anyway?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I don't know. It seems to me now that I had an opportunity of seeing a paper which was printed and published by the Roma community. And you know, the Roma generally speaking are apolitical. They don't care much about politics anyway. Croats and Muslims are much too fearful to expose themselves to any risk involved in such an enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The leaders amongst the Muslims and the leaders amongst the Croats, if they wanted to reach out to people and communicate with them, what possibilities were there and how did they go about it? Because I take it that you're telling us that they had no newspapers, neither openly nor underground, nor clandestinely. So if they wanted to reach their people, how did they do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: To be frank, I don't know. I kept a diary, that is true. But I was never able to realise in what way they communicated to their people, if they actually did. As a Croat, in those days, I wasn't even aware of who the Croatian leader was. There was a man by the name of Jovic, but I never saw him. I don't know what he looks like. And I think that as far as Muslims are concerned, they held several press conferences at the time. They tried to protest, but to no avail, with the exception, perhaps, of Muharem Krzic, the president of the SDA, who miraculously appeared on the TV on a couple of occasions, the Banja Luka TV. However, it later turned out that he was their player which they used in order to be able to say that it was actually a democratic society, a democratic community, despite the fact that lots of rumours were going around against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the region, in the area that you are familiar with, apart from TV Banja Luka and TV Pale, were there any other stations that could -- that were received?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: The Belgrade TV, which was our Bible, was supposed to be like our Bible. They were the ones who knew the real truth and the only truth, and they had to be obeyed. The local players were only puppets who acted pursuant to their instructions. And I'm referring to the local people in Banja Luka and elsewhere in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. So you say TV Banja Luka, TV Pale, TV Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- TV Belgrade. And are you in a position to tell us which of these three stations was mostly followed or followed most?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I think the Banja Luka TV because of the local patriotism. We all wanted to watch our TV. Then the Pale TV was also widely watched because of Risto Dzogo, a journalist, who would eventually be killed by the Serbs themselves, who made a number of tasteless appearances on TV and displayed shameful primitivism to the extent that it's hard to understand. I mean, if you were to watch one such shows featuring Risto Dzogo, may God rest his soul, everything would be really made clear to you. You would really remain speechless after seeing a programme of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Radio Banja Luka is also one medium that you mentioned. Were there any other radio stations that you are aware of that you can mention to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: There was a very important radio station called BIG radio station. This particular radio station broadcast the music that appealled to the people, the kind of music that everyone liked, pop music, blues, and jazz, whereas the Banja Luka radio was not as appealing to the local population as this particular radio station. But once the war started, this radio station called BIG radio would also turn the coat and join in the propaganda and play a part in everything that was taking place at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you back to what you said on the 24th of June now. And you said: "Who would have heard Mr. Brdjanin speaking, had it not been for," and let's take them one by one. Radio Banja Luka. Can you confirm to us that you heard Mr. Brdjanin speaking on Radio Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, by all means I can confirm that. He spoke on the radio constantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]....

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I think you can see this from my diary. I made notes of that, at least once a week. I do not want to make a mistake. But on the top of my head, I think it was once a week. The most frequent guests were Brdjanin, Lukic, and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And BIG radio station, did you ever hear Mr. Brdjanin speak on BIG radio station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember. I don't believe that he didn't, but I cannot say that he did. But at any rate, if he did speak on that radio station, it would be noted in my diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, TV Banja Luka, his appearance on TV Banja Luka, can you confirm that, or reconfirm that? How often did it occur? Do we rely on what you have in your diary, or can you expand on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I mostly rely on my diary, but he did appear very often. For instance, the programme called "Open Screen" with Nikola Deretic, he appeared on that programme, and he was asked what to do with the so-called national equation, and then he said: "Well, we will take a Croat, and then a Serb."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't quite get. We will take a Croat, and then a Serb, and do what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: No. It was only for purely formalistic reasons. He didn't want to take a Muslim or a Croat but a less valuable Serb, such as persons who were baptised only later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, yes. TV Pale. Do you recall Brdjanin appearing on TV Pale?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Without looking at my notes, it's difficult for me to recall. I believe he did appear. There were many phone-in programmes. He was perhaps at the studio in Banja Luka, but would also appear on the Pale-based TV. It probably involved cooperation between two studios or two TV stations. I'm not sure, but I know that he did appear on that TV as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we proceed any further, now his interventions on Radio Banja Luka, can you place these in a time frame? Are we talking of 1992, of 1993, both? 1991? 1994? When are we -- when did you hear Mr. Brdjanin take part in Radio Banja Luka programmes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Again, relying on my diary, because it covers the year of 1992 all the way to the 19th of November 1993, so I can only talk about that period, I -- after that I no longer listened to it, so I cannot talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I want from you is a confirmation or a denial that when you say that you heard him speak on Radio Banja Luka, you are referring to 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993. Those two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And TV Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: TV Banja Luka, also during that period. Nothing later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: TV Pale?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: That, too. All my knowledge, everything that I can talk about here, concerns 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You do confirm that you recall his appearance on TV Banja Luka and TV Pale, in particular the last one, in 1992? In 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And TV Belgrade? Did you ever see Mr. Brdjanin on TV Belgrade? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I cannot remember that at this point. I think that I saw him on TV Novi Sad when the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared, and I believe that there was discussion about that on TV Novi Sad, that the event was described as a seminal event. As for Belgrade TV, I don't know, but I'm sure he did appear on Belgrade TV as well because they were often taken there. They were some sort of attraction because they were supposed to implement the unification of a whole country with Serbia. The Belgrade TV, I think this would have been either in 1993 or maybe 1994. There was a programme called "Thank you for the Krajina, Banja Luka," they were expressing their gratitude for having attained Krajina. Radio Belgrade and Radio Banja Luka shot this programme jointly, so they were expressing their gratitude for this, whereas we, at the same time, were being forced to leave the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Brdjanin in the media now. Again, I would like to refer you, Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman, to page 18.013 of the transcript. And this is the witness testifying on the 23rd of June 2003 with reference to the entry in his diary of the 28th of August 1992. Now, you said something which is very strong indeed here with regard to the accused. You said: "But for -- as for Brdjanin, he thought he was God's gift to the masses." I'm not much concerned with this, but I'm very much concerned on what follows. You then said: "He decided on life and death." Why did you say that? What do you mean by it? Because although you later say he thought that was his right: "I'm not saying here that he really wanted bad things to happen to Croats and Muslims, I don't want to say that. But the way he addressed himself, the way he spoke, and his public announcements in the mass media, the way he spoke, he caused panic among the people. That's what he did. That's a fact." But I put it to you that speaking in a way as to cause panic amongst the people should not drive you to the conclusion that he decided on life and death. That's a very, very strong statement that you made with regard to Brdjanin. So could you please explain to us why you stated that he decided on life and death.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I'll do my best to clarify, if I'm able to. If a national leader appearing before a heated mass of people says: "We're going to fight for our people, and within the next hundred years we will expel all of -- pagans from our area," it's clear what he means. If Your Honours were to listen to a speech of that kind, it would be easy for you to reject it. But if an uneducated person listens to such a leader, a credulous, uneducated person, he is prepared to do everything, and indeed to take arms against those pagans. Oftentimes when I would run into a Muslim friend in the street and ask him how he was, I would get an answer: "I'm doing fine, but I'm afraid of the dark. I'm afraid of the night," because miracles happened, terrible things happened in those days. And this is how I see it. This is what I meant when I said that he was deciding on the life and death of people, because through his extremism, he encouraged, he incited the madmen who would engage eventually in doing horrible things which made us so infamous today in the world and ruined otherwise good reputation which we had enjoyed prior to this terrible war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 49, line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The witness said: "Within the next 100 years." And the hundred didn't make it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, okay. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Because I did notice that as well and I realised why you are standing up. When did he make -- let's skip that, because we have a reference to that. Do you mean, because again, this is very important, what responsibility are you attributing to Mr. Brdjanin for what happened? When you tell us: "He decided on life and death," at the same time, you're telling us: "I am not saying here that he really wanted bad things to happen to Croats and Muslims," it seems on the face of it to amount to -- not exactly a contradiction in terms, but one annihilates the other, to an extent. Where do we stand with you? You're talking of Brdjanin giving us the impression that you know enough to be able to make such statements on him. What responsibility are you attributing to him for what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: In my opinion, he is most responsible for the fact that he was irresponsible, for not having thought twice about things that he was going to say. He never thought of the consequences that his speeches might give rise to, and this is something that I would hold most against him. Undoubtedly, he's a clever, intelligent man who should have known what sort of an impression his passionate speeches would have on these rather primitive people, sometimes even antisocial people. Certainly, most of the events took place as a result of his encouragement addressed to the extremists who were to commit atrocious things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you be specific here? Such as? I tried to explain to you why I'm putting these questions to you, because if I make a speech and I make a mistake in my speech and I realise, without realising that I am inciting the people, and then as a result of my speech something happens that I did not want, I did not anticipate, I did not desire, and it happens, I will take all necessary steps that next time I will try and do exactly the opposite, rather than incite, and I will be very cautious with the choice of my words. What did exactly happen? This is what I want to know. Because I would imagine that everyone knew what was happening. I mean, if you knew it, if the man -- ordinary man in the street was aware of what was happening, I suppose that even Mr. Brdjanin, one would conclude or assume that Mr. Brdjanin knew what was happening. So what was the result of all this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: This is what I was talking about when I said that he decided on matters of life and death, because had a man thought of himself committing a mistake when saying these things, becoming aware of the consequences, he would have changed his tone of speeches. But this is not what he did. He was convinced of practically paying a service to the Serbs by talking this way, which was quite untrue. All of his speeches resonated with hatred, and I'm sure you are aware of this as well. And that is why I said that he was responsible for the evil, he committed evil. He incited people to commit evil things. And that is what I meant when I said that he decided about the fates of people. That is certainly a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And according to you did he incite people to commit those things? Can you give us instances when? Can you give us understands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: For instance, when he said at one of the meetings that these heathens, that we should get rid of them, we should strike them off the soles of our feet. There was the second instance when we were talking about the leveling to be done amongst the peoples. "We'll take a Serb. We won't take a Muslim. We won't take a Croat. We'd rather take a Serb who is less valuable because he was baptised later on in his life," although all of these gentlemen were once members of the old party and were baptised later on. Franjo Tudjman went to see the Pope, and he actually had his old father baptised at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Taya would like you to be more specific with regard to the time frame.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: As for the time frame, as I said, this was from the very beginning, but I can talk about 1992 up until November 1993. I cannot talk about the events prior to or after the mentioned period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do I take it, reading through your diary and re-reading through your testimony and also what you told us this afternoon, that Mr. Brdjanin was making prolific use of the mass media? Is this your assessment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if this is your assessment, may I ask you also what your assessment is with regard to the next question, whether he was using the mass media as an instrument for his own advancement or whether your assessment leads you to the conclusion that he was using the mass media in pursuance of a broader agenda, an agenda which went beyond his own personal one? Which one would you say? I don't want you to speculate. If you are not sure, if you don't know, please don't -- just say so. But if you can make an assessment and let us have it, then proceed. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I am inclined to believe that most of the things that he did do he did them for his own advancement, that this was his priority. As a leader, I believe -- or actually I'm quite convinced on the basis of my knowledge about him and on the basis of what I heard from others about him, I am convinced that there was his personal ambition that he was driven by. Such an opportunity appears once in a lifetime that enables you to become from a common citizen the person number one in a country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But how do you reconcile some of the statements that you attributed to Mr. Brdjanin on TV Banja Luka and on the radio and also in the papers with his self-advancement or his own agenda?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: How to reconcile them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll tell you why. He already occupied quite some important positions at the time. Like, we hear president of the ARK Crisis Staff, was deputy vice-president of the region, of the ARK...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Somewhere I read a Bosnian saying which would answer to your question. It says as follows: "Bosnian, if he made a great career somewhere on the North Pole, this would come to nothing for him unless he came back to Bosnia to boast about it." So in other words, he was pleased whenever he heard someone saying: "This is what Brdjanin said," and this was the drive that took him forward, and I believe that his ambitions did exceed the position of the president of the regional -- of the region of Krajina. I am quite certain about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you're basically telling us that mostly you would say that Brdjanin used the mass media as an instrument for self-advancement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: This is my opinion [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your opinion, your assessment. In other words, you are ruling out that he was using the mass media as a tool in the hands of others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
