utterances.text: To put it frankly, I don't really believe that. Perhaps sometimes he did implement an order arriving from Pale, because quite often he was in conflict with the Pale people, Karadzic and Krajisnik. Very often, there was friction between them, and even in such situations he would appear and give statements. Perhaps some statements that were to his detriment in such a situation. Perhaps he did sometimes implement some of the instructions given to him, but for the most part I believe he acted autonomously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically my question is this: He was speaking for himself. Was he speaking for the SDS, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did, although the SDS was also full of factions. Because you see, this was a group of political laymen, so to say, who advocated some sort of an agenda. They all said: "We, Serbs, are going to be number one." Even Karadzic said that God was a Serb. But amongst themselves, there was a rivalry of a sort. This was -- this primitive, rural logic. They liked listening to the people saying how they said something -- put something nicely or said something that appealed to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the way you have put it to us, you seem to suggest to us that basically the media was manipulated in favour -- by and in favour of the Serbian cause. Is that correct? Centrally operated and manipulated to further the Serbian cause. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. For --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How does Brdjanin fit into that? If he was, according to you, mostly interested in using the mass media in furtherance -- to further his own self-advancement, how does he fit in with the Serbian agenda?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Whether he was player of such a league, well, I'm not even sure that he was as interested in that as much. They were all struggling to assume their place on the stage, to become significant and distinguish themselves from the mass. How does he fit into all that? In the very beginning when control was assumed over the mass media, his role was not a significant one. The -- it was Miro Mladjenovic, Andjelko Grahovac and others who took part in assuming control over the mass media. If you allow me, Your Honours, I have here an example testifying to the struggle for the media. If you allow me to read it out briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Where are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I am reading from my diary, entry on Saturday, 18th of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we have to...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Here's what it says here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: It reads as follows: "During the day, the director of Crna agency has called Radio Sarajevo on several occasions asking from the people responsible for that media to switch off their programme on the mid-waves because they wanted to broadcast their programme on that particular wave. He threatened that unless they did so, he would issue a missile, he would send a missile on their particular building. At 17 hours and 17 minutes -- 22 minutes, the presenter stopped the reporting of news and gave the following announcement to the viewers, that the Radio and Television Sarajevo building was being shelled that very moment. Following a brief consultation with the editor, Slobodan Trbojevic -" I believe; it is hard to read in this particular spot in my diary - "...it was decided that the programme would continue and the editor himself stated the following at the end of the programme: `The following news programme will be precisely at 7.30 p.m. Of course, if we'll still be alive.`." This indicates the scope, the proportions that this action for the assumption of control over the mass media was. They imposed some sort of a blockade that they later on left it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour,, there are two transcript corrections. And I'm almost -- I think both of them -- well, no, one of them is still there but it will be gone in just a second. 54:6. Page 54, line 6 -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now it's gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I'll get there. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He says something -- I haven't got it here any longer. He says something like: "That's my opinion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "This is my opinion."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm told he actually said was: "This is my conviction."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's be specific, precise on this. I had told you, Witness: "So you're basically telling us that mostly you would say that Brdjanin used the mass media as an instrument for self-advancement." And you said: "This is my conviction," or, "This is my opinion." Are you convinced of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 55:16, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment now because I have to go further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's a sentence ending with: "Significant one." Then in that space before it starts talking about people, I'm told that he said: "I do not want to attribute that to him."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I have to read out to the witness what he said. And then he tells me whether he said the words: "I do not want to attribute that to him." "You're talking of Brdjanin. Whether he was a player of such a league, well, I am not even sure he was as interested in that as much. They were all struggling to assume their place on the stage to become significant and distinguish themselves from the masses. How does he fit into all that? In the very beginning, when control was assumed over the mass media, his role was not a significant one." What I want to know, before you mention Miro Mladjenovic is, "I do not want to attribute that to him." Did you say these words, to start with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I don't know if I said this, to tell you the truth. But when I said that I did not want to attribute this to him, what I meant was that I don't want to attribute to him a role that he did not have in this media grabbing. I don't know if I was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think it's clear enough, Mr. Ackerman. I think it's clear. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, you were recounting to us what you entered in your diary on the 18th of April, and you were in the point of explaining that following, "A brief consultation with the editors, Slobodan Trbojevic, I believe. It's hard to read in this particular spot in my diary. It was decided that the programme would continue and the editor himself stated the following, 'The end of the programme, the following news programme will be at precisely 7.30 p.m., of course, if we'll still be alive'." And then you were interrupted -- well, you also added: "This indicates for control over the mass media was, they imposed some sort of a blockade which they..." And then you were interrupted. We would like you to conclude on this and tell us what your conclusion is. What does this event indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I thought that I finished talking about this particular event. I want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It did not come through in the transcript also because you were interrupted. So if you can repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: This instance of 17th of April serves to illustrate how vigorously they fought for the media, for the space on the media, because the media allowed you to promote yourself and to say whatever it was you wanted to say. In this sense, I mentioned Bogdan Bogdanovic who was unable to be heard at the time, whereas those who brandished their weapons would be on the TV day and night. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you to another part of your testimony, and I am -- please refer to the entry in your diary for the 5th of May 1992. Now, there you are referring to what, according to you, Brdjanin was reported as saying; namely, that all those who are contemplating leaving Bosanska Krajina, regardless of whether they are Serbs, Croats, or Muslims, will be simply warned, and other parts of Serbia, and perhaps Montenegro, will be told not to accept them. They should not be leaving these parts now when they are needed most by the people. I am allowing -- and those in the crisis area to save their children." Then when you were referred to this part of your 5th May entry, in your testimony, page 18.086, you testified as follows: You said: "You needed to be there to sense the atmosphere and understand what these things really meant, what the words meant to the people." We seem a little bit -- we feel a little bit uncertain about what to understand by this. Can you explain further. We don't want an explanation on what Mr. Brdjanin according to you is reported as having said. But how do you tie that up with what you testified? You needed to be there to sense the atmosphere and understand what these things really meant, what the words meant to the people. In other words, if he's telling, "Don't leave." And others will be asked not to accept you because we need you here, where do they fit in or tie up together, especially within a context of an alleged ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: When I said you had to be there to sense it, I was referring to one specific thing. If -- throughout that time I was suffering traumas caused by provocations, telephone ringing at midnight, someone telling over the phone: "Ustasha, balija, you should leave here," and if I listened to the same person saying: "Well, why shouldn't we have concentration camps if Stalin and Hitler had them, why couldn't we have them," and so on, and then if I hear from this same person something that is supposed to put my mind at ease, well, it's not going to work this way. I'm not going to feel at ease. So why should I be there to stand guard or whatever at this concentration camp? Why should I stay here and support this state if I am not a second-rate but a tenth-rate citizen. If you know the people out there who have nothing to live on, who are being thrown out of their flats because they dodged the mobilisation call-up, then you cannot find any comfort in the nice words you hear from such people because people don't trust them. All his deeds renege whatever nice utterings or well-meaning words he might say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but why would Mr. Brdjanin -- let me put it to you in a different manner. The Prosecution is alleging that Mr. Brdjanin was a part of a joint criminal enterprise which had on its agenda the ethnic cleansing of the non-Serbs from the Bosanska Krajina. If he was indeed a part of that agenda, and he is almost threatening Croats and Muslims, apart from Serbs, not to leave, why would he say so? Why would he speak out like this in these terms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: It must have depended on the biorhythm. It's difficult for me to answer your question. He was probably part of them. Essentially, it was a huge conspiracy in which he was involved, a conspiracy against Bosnia and Herzegovina and against Croatia. Events first took place in Croatia, and then they spilled over into Bosnia. We cannot forecast or second-guess what would have happened had the west not intervened, and it's difficult to tell at this point where we would have been today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does the fact that this entry goes back to the 5th of May 1992 have any significance at all considering what he is saying? What happened on the 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: To be perfectly frank, I would have to read the entry to know what happened on the 5th of May. He had an interview with Stegic on that day, if this is what you're referring to. All of our days were more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much involvement was there already at the time on the part of the international community regarding the allegations that were rife on ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: The involvement of the international community, I don't quite understand your question, Your Honour. I don't know what exactly you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I have in mind is this: That more or less while you were testifying on this, you also said: "This was putting in the measuring rod and seeing how the international community would react. Whenever there was a sharp reaction from the international community, they would immediately quiet down a little bit and watch for reactions from the international community. As soon as reactions were reserved, they would step up, step up the whole thing, and that was the truth of it."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have the page, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 18.088. 18.086, okay, because I have a number missing here. It's handwritten.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Now I see what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I want from you is whether there is a connection between the two. In other words, when you said that Mr. Brdjanin -- when you entered in your diary what Mr. Brdjanin is reported as having said, at the same time you're telling us in your testimony you can't imagine, you needed to be there to see, to understand what these things really meant. And then within the same context, you mention also the reactions to the international community. Are you combining them together, or is it just by accident that you referred us to the international community and reactions to -- the reactions of the international community, counter-reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the context in which this can be placed. But I think we have the same thing in mind. Whenever an extreme statement was made, a statement which would shock any normal human and civilised being, immediately after that a press conference would be organised where attempts were made at playing down the initial statement. So the pulse of the international community was being felt, so to speak. However, the international community, being unaware and uninformed of our history and the character of our people, repeated the same mistakes with Milosevic as they did with Hitler 50 years before that. So concessions were made in the hope that they would be able to put an end to all these events. However, eventually when it was clear that the international community was not prepared to intervene and that they would leave Bosnia at its own fate, then they started engaging in what they eventually did. So international forces only later were able to get into the country. I'm referring to the peacekeeping force which in the end interposed themselves between the warring factions. But this is the heritage that is going to be very difficult to dispel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've still not cleared this up for us. You yourself told us and others told us here that there were instances when Mr. Brdjanin made speeches to the effect that not more than so many, such a percentage of Muslims will remain in the region, in the area. Anyone who would have heard Mr. Brdjanin say that, if he said that, and then hear Mr. Brdjanin say what you report here on the 5th of May would ask the question: "Has he changed his policy, is he crazy? First he tells us there should be little or no Muslims left here, and now he is telling them 'don't -- you leave because we will' -- so if he is saying something which is diametrically opposed to what he had stated before, according to you and others, why would he be saying this? Is it because -- are you hinting, in other words, that he said this because there was pressure from the international community at the time? This is what we want to know. Or is it just because consistency is not exactly one of the best virtues of politicians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: You are certainly right about that. It did play a role. I tried to cover as best as I could what he said or wrote down. I entered everything into my diary. I did hear Mr. Brdjanin speak. I'm not sure he was referring only to Muslims on those occasions; however, he was mentioning the number -- the figure of five per cent of non-Serbs who would be allowed to stay. The rest had to pack and go. At least this is how we interpreted what he said. Mr. Brdjanin even had a custom when he was in good mood of telling stories about his Muslim friends in a rather positive manner and over the radio. Unfortunately, those were very rare occasions which could not counteract or undo what he had previously said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Janu has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I would just like to know if you can recall at this time when those statements were produced, can you recall whether already these agencies for replacement, exchange of population operating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: This would have been at the beginning of 1992, yes, certainly. Yes. However, the departures were not en masse, but a large number of people already left. Now, as to how we were aware of that, because we were not receiving any information to that effect, I, as a Catholic, often went to the local cemetery. Before the war, at the local cemetery, one would see many candles burning. But once the war broke out, you could see that there were much less candles burning at the local cemetery. And this is how we concluded that that portion of the population had left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 64, line 6, the line interpreted "What he said," and then after that full stop. I'm told the witness said: "And later he was saying,`stay here'."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I may have said it, but I don't want to commit myself. I know that he would first say one thing, and then another, and then it was difficult for a person to make up his or her mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I'm going back to my question because--

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't answered your question. What he want to know is whether, in fact, you had stated: "The rest had to pack and go, at least this is how we interpreted what he said. And later he was saying `stay here'." Did you say: "And later he was saying `stay here'," when you were testifying here today, a few minutes ago. Because Mr. Ackerman is alleging that the transcript stops when you had actually continued to say: "And later he was saying `stay here'." Do you remember saying the words: "And later he was saying `stay here'."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe in the context of what I was saying, but from time to time he would say a positive thing, or that he would first say something negative and then something positive. I don't know. It is possible that I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- just a moment. I think that if Mr. Ackerman wants to make his corrections, the answer is for his case manager to tell him immediately that something -- and then it should be stopped then. Because clearly six questions answered -- I mean, who can remember what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not six questions. But, still, I mean your suggestion is a practical one. Yes, Mr. Ackerman. You're telling me you wouldn't like to interrupt the witness when he was still answering a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's for sure. But I wait until the witness is finished. But the other thing, this is important enough that I would like that passage marked and I would like the tape checked because I'm quite certain my case manager is right, that he said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be attended to, Mr. Ackerman. Yes, Judge Janu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: It looks like a paradox if these agencies for replacement or exchange of population were working, and they were working, in my opinion, with the consent of the authorities, would be organising this exchange and at the same time Mr. Brdjanin, as a representative of authority, high-positioned authority, would say: "Don't leave, and I am allowing just the children to be sent away." Nobody else. So I cannot just reconcile these two statements of yours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: You see, we can get the children out and take them to safety. Now, if the children are not safe in the area, then it tells you a lot about the situation. It was not my comment. I think that it was a quote that I heard. I cannot remember the exact quote. It is true that Brdjanin could say from time to time something that would have pleasantly surprised you. As I have already indicated, he sometimes talked about his Muslims friends in a positive manner. However, if that was preceded by a dozen of -- threats addressed to you, then you cannot take it in that manner. Now, if he says: "Stay here, take up arms," and defend this imaginary country of his, I mean, why would I do a thing like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a suspicion that his statement may have had something to do with the mobilisation which was given a lot of importance and publicity on that same day. If that is the case, would you change your explanation? Look at your entry of the 5th of May of 1992. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: While he's looking my inquiry is if do you intend to break and then come back and finish by 6.30, or how do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I definitely intend to finish by 6.30. I was expecting Madam Registrar to tell me what time to break because I'm a little bit lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That doesn't make sense. It doesn't make sense. So shall we stop for 15 minutes now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, rather than doing that, I mean, we didn't sit again until 5.30 -- or 4.30. So why don't we just continue and leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would very willingly do that, but I don't want to impose on --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. If Your Honours -- it seems to me, it never is 15 minutes, so by the time we had all reassembled, it would hardly be worth it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What time did we start again, Madam Chuqing? After the break, what time did we start again? But what time was it when we started?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: After this last break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 4.30. So in 10 minutes' time we would have been sitting for half an hour. Can we proceed for a little bit more and then call it a day? I want to know if I have the okay from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Just have a look at your entry of the 5th of May, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, I've had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm trying to make some sense out of it. It's not normal for people --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: It is directly linked to the issue of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you exclude now the link with the reaction that there could have been at the time from the international community? Because it can't be both. It's either one or the other.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, Your Honour, at this point, my concentration is failing me. I have not read the whole document. I can tell that we're talking about mobilisation here, but with your permission I should like to have the opportunity of reading the whole thing, which I'm prepared to do tonight.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I suggest, really in fairness to him, that's something I was trying to achieve yesterday. If Your Honours would give him overnight the list -- or give us the list of the diary entries you are going to be referring tomorrow so he can reread it in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There aren't much more, but I can -- I can do that, and thank you for suggesting it, Ms. Korner. We can, actually. This you will come again to us tomorrow after having consulted your... Now, I refer you to your testimony on the 24th of June 2003, reference 18.076. And you're now answering questions on cross-examination. And in reply to a question that was put to you by Mr. Ackerman, you said: "Yes, you cannot just say that it is just Mr. Brdjanin who was creating the atmosphere and raising the tension which would then result in the misfortune that occurred, but the fact is that he is one of them, that is certain, and there is no doubt about that whatsoever." You are certainly implying here that there were others who were creating this atmosphere and fermenting tension. Who were the others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: For example, Dr. Vukic, Radislav Vukic; he was terrible. Predrag Radic, the mayor of Banja Luka. Vojo Kupresanin, Andjelko Grahovac at the very beginning. He's the only person from the town who joined the gang. Then Miro Mladjenovic, the editor of the Glas, and then Professor Predrag Lazarevic who would become the president of the Serbian intellectuals of Banja Luka who said once when he took the stage: "In these days, it is the birth certificate that best describes a person." So those were the kind of people who were engaged in these things. Not all of them were publicly exposed such as Vukic and Brdjanin, but they all made their own contribution to the misfortune that befell us. There were many others, such as Kasagic and many more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And out of all these persons that you've mentioned and others that you may not have mentioned, who in your opinion or in your assessment spoke with the most authority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Well, I think the one who spoke with the most authority was perhaps Professor Lazarevic. He was a true intellectual unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, what --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Radic also had a certain amount of authority. Many of them had turned coats and became national -- and rode the national tidewave [as interpreted]. They felt that their time had come, but at the same time they only had their own private gain in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When I'm referring to most authority, I'm referring to political power, someone who speaks. For example, was Professor Lazarevic a person in authority? Or was he just an intellectual and people respected him as an intellectual? I'm not asking about that. I'm asking about who amongst this list of persons that you mentioned to us spoke with authority, with the highest? Who amongst them spoke most with authority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I think the four that I mentioned and whom I describe as the four writers of the apocalypse. Kupresanin, Radic, Brdjanin, and Vukic. They spoke with authority from the positions of power. However, in my personal conviction, Professor Lazarevic was equally evil because he also enjoyed authority and respect, and he perhaps encouraged the others to say something that otherwise they would not have said. But once again, the four that I mentioned, they spoke with authority from the positions of power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the one who spoke most vehemently, with most vehemency, who would you say it would be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I cannot decide between Vukic and Brdjanin. Vukic when he was drunk, he would say all kinds of things, and he was usually drunk. Brdjanin was also outspoken, but he had a certain rhetoric in mind. And his speeches were morbid, whereas in the case of Vukic, you could tell that he was an idiot. He was retarded, and he was laughed at by those, by the people who were recording his speeches. Whereas, on the other hand, Brdjanin looked much more serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who amongst the two that you mentioned, Vukic and -- who used the strongest terms? Forgetting that one of them, according to you, was inebriated when he made some speeches. He couldn't have been inebriated, drunk, all the time. I mean, I have met people like that in my life. Who out of the two would use the strongest terms when they were both sober?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I am not aware of Brdjanin ever having been drunk at those public appearances. As for Lukic [as interpreted], he not only drank; he gorged himself on alcohol. When he was drunk, he would say all kinds of things. Brdjanin was never drunk or inebriated, but he could say ugly things, really ugly things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we just try and correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't watching the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It came through the interpretation as well. It came through as Lukic, and I don't think he said Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. It was my mistake, Your Honour. It was Vukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move. Please refer Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Korner to page 18.169, and this is you testifying again, sir. You say: "In the context of the ARK, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, he" - you're referring to Mr. Brdjanin - "he was certainly quite a big player. As for Republika Srpska, I think even there he was near the top, near the very top. It's difficult for me to say, but I think he was near the top. After all, he was a man who dared to even oppose Karadzic himself sometimes." I want this clarified. Are you coming to the conclusion or did you come to the conclusion that he was near the top or very near the top because on occasions he even dared to oppose Karadzic himself? Or do you have other information or sources of information that would convince you to repeat three times that -- three times in a few seconds that you are convinced that he was near the top?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I am convinced that he was indeed near the top, and that is illustrated in his confrontation with Karadzic, not about any central or vital issues. But for instance, what is going to be the capital of Republika Srpska, whether it's going to be Pale or Banja Luka. That's what they confronted each other about. And Brdjanin was able to say well, it's not going to be this way, it's going to be the other way. Now, that they confronted each other or not on matters, I don't believe so. They shared the same plan. It was only this unfortunate issue of whether Banja Luka or Pale or Sarajevo were going to be the capital. In any case, he resisted Karadzic's idea that Sarajevo be the capital. I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's not because you have additional information, other information that would make you link Mr. Brdjanin with the top?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Top, the way I saw him, he was always very much publicly exposed. Whenever there was a Serbian Assembly, if you judge it by this, of course he will not ask for the opinion of some of those insignificant people. Sometimes he wouldn't even ask Karadzic but would ask Brdjanin. At least I'm speaking about the Banja Luka TV, when you judge by the way journalists approached him, it is -- they sometimes weigh the importance of the figures when they -- when they're deciding about who to interview. For Karadzic and the other man - what's his name - Krajisnik, well, they would certainly ask Brdjanin to give his opinion rather more frequently than Radic or Vukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 72, line 15, at the period, "It's going to be the other way." I'm told that he then said "It was not so easy to say `no' to Radovan."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you say that? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you the last question for today, and then I will give you some idea of what we will be asking you tomorrow, and then you can go back to your hotel and rest. On the 15th of July, you made an entry in your diary to which you referred in the course of your testimony and to which you referred a few minutes ago. I mean, I'm taking you back to when you described Brdjanin as part of the three horsemen of the riders of the apocalypse, and the others being Kupresanin, Vukic, and Radic. You also stated in your testimony of the 24th of June 2003 at page 18.167 that out of the four riders of the horsemen of the apocalypse, Brdjanin was without a shadow of doubt the one who appeared most in the media. And then you said something again which intrigued us a little bit. This led you to the conclusion that Brdjanin took the most - this is what you said - "fatal decisions since these were communicated through the media by him." Now, let's forget about the "fatal" for a moment because "fatal" has got its own connotations. Who was taking these decisions, these decisions that he was communicating, according to you, through the media? Because -- let me -- the way I read it, the way I read it, you're not saying there were these four horsemen of the apocalypse, and each one of them was communicating the decisions taken by them or by someone through the media. You're saying that they were four horsemen of the apocalypse - you mentioned them - of whom it was Brdjanin who appeared most in the media; it was Brdjanin who took the most fatal decisions, took the most fatal decisions since these were communicated through the media by him. And what were the others doing? Who was taking these decisions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Let me tell you: These four persons were the nucleus of power in the town. They decided about everything relating to the very town of Banja Luka. They probably had some instructions from Pale, from those above. They were in communication. I'm not saying that a specific decision was taken by Radoslav Brdjanin; but among the four, the decision was indeed taken. And normally, he would present the decision. That's why I said that he would be the one to disclose the decision of a sort, and that is why I highlighted him as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you say it was these same circumstances that led you to the conclusion that Brdjanin took the most fatal decisions, since these were communicated through the media by him, do you mean to tell us that the decisions actually were not necessarily his, but they were the combined -- the joint --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm so sorry. Before Your Honour goes on, I simply cannot see what Your Honour is looking at. All I can see on the transcript is "Most of the fatal decisions were taken by Brdjanin." Where does Your Honour see it was communicated through the media? I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I'm asking. Are you saying this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Because at the moment -- I understood you to be reading that he said this before, but he hasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. What I am putting to him is that now that he is telling us that the decisions were taken conjointly and not by Mr. Brdjanin, does he stand by his statement that since it was Brdjanin who mostly appeared in the media communicating these decisions, that the perception from the public would be that it is Brdjanin who is taking these decisions? What were you exactly saying? Because this is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: In fact, the public thought that he was the one taking the decisions. Now, to what degree his role went in taking the decisions, I cannot say. But I think that most of the, so to say, "ugly" decisions that related to us specifically, well, he was the one who presented them. And I'm not saying that this automatically meant that he was the one who decided upon these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is what you told us way back on the 24th of June, that -- if you read what you stated on the 24th of June, one might get carried away with the idea that you were saying -- that you were telling us that the most fatal decisions were actually taken by Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm so sorry. But really, what he actually said was: "Most of the fatal decisions, at least the way it seemed, were taken by Brdjanin. I am not sure if that was only an outward representation of his power and his desire to be in the forefront."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I'm asking whether this is a perception that the public and whoever watched the media at the time must have got or probably got simply because it was Brdjanin who was appearing more often than the others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Precisely. This is the impression one would get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we'll stop here for today. I would like you to -- do you have a pen nearby? Yes, I would like him to make some notes on what we will be asking him tomorrow. Perhaps he can check. Now, entry 9th April 1992, when you draw a comparison between Glas and Goebbels' Volkischer Beobachter? We will ask you to clarify that for us. 15th July 1992, you say that you spoke to Miro Mladjenovic trying to encourage him in his fight against the powerful triumvirate... et cetera. How could you reconcile you going to Glas and encourage Mladjenovic when you were comparing his paper to Goebbels Volkischer Beobachter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I can give you an answer immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, tomorrow. Because everyone has a right to a rest. And then you refer also to the pressure which was exerted on Mladjenovic. We want more details on that. And we also want details as to whether the editorial policy of Glas changed at all following his removal, and whether what happened to Glas was just particular to Glas or whether it happened also with regard to other newspapers. Am I running too fast for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you had an entry on the 4th of August 1992 where you make reference to the red van in Banja Luka. We would like to know whether the existence of this red van was reported in the media at the time. And if so, how widely. And then your entry of the 11th August wherein you refer to your knowledge of the laws that prevented Muslims from moving around in Celinac. We want to know how you came by this information. And then finally, you will recall -- page 18.180 of the transcript, for the benefit of counsel. You recall testifying about a man who got beaten when you brought him to a doctor, and we have a picture, a photo of him. We would like more information on the event, also about his ethnicity, because that did not come out in the course of your testimony. And always, with regard to this particular incident, whether you recall any reports in the media on it or on similar incidents that you may be aware of. So we'll give you a rest --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Excuse me. What was this -- the date, that is, this incident about the man being beaten up, which entry should I look at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, there is no entry. It's you refer to this incident in your testimony. If necessary, we can print out the excerpt from page 18 -- but he won't understand it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Fine, fine. Fine. I will find my way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman. I see you standing for a reason or?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I would just like a note made and the tape checked, page 75, line 20. It's believed that he said: "Perhaps those decisions were taken by someone else", there at the end of line 20. I would just like the tape to be checked and a note to be made about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine. Okey-dokey. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one other thing. Because the witness thought that, as we all did, it was going to be fairly quick, he has arranged to have dinner with someone from the office, nobody connected with our team. Now, it's a matter for Your Honours whether Your Honours wish to allow him to do this on the strict understanding he cannot discuss the evidence, or prefer to tell them he should not do it.
